H: On television, he is the king of the dead. A crown of ice grows from his skull. He raises armies with a lift of his arms, and when he finally falls, every dead thing in the world falls with him. But George R. R. Martin's books tell a very different story. In the books, the Night's King was a man. A brother of the Night's Watch, who fell in love with a woman whose skin was white as the moon, and whose eyes were like blue stars. When it was over, his name was erased from history. So who was he really?
P: On the Wall stands the oldest castle of the Night's Watch, and the largest. They call it the Nightfort. Its towers are broken. Its halls are full of rats and dust. For two hundred years, no brother has lived there. When young Bran Stark shelters inside its walls, he remembers the stories his old nurse told him about this place. Here, the Rat Cook served a king a pie made from the king's own son. Here, the seventy-nine sentinels were sealed into the ice for deserting, and still stand watch, facing north. And here, before all of them, Night's King had reigned, until his name was wiped from the memory of man.
I: The story begins at the end of the Long Night, a winter that lasted a generation. When the darkness finally broke, men raised a Wall of ice seven hundred feet high. Legend says it was built by Brandon the Builder, the first Stark king, with the help of giants and the children of the forest. And they founded a brotherhood to guard it. The Night's Watch: men who took no wives, held no lands, and fathered no children. The Night's King was the thirteenth man to lead them. Old Nan said he was a warrior who knew no fear. "And that was the fault in him," she would add, "for all men must know fear." Fear is what keeps a man on top of the Wall, watching the dark. A man who fears nothing might look at the dark and want to walk into it.
II: One night, from the top of the Wall, he saw her. A woman with skin as white as the moon and eyes like blue stars. Fearing nothing, he chased her, and caught her, and loved her, though her skin was cold as ice. And with his love, Old Nan said, he gave her his soul. The books never say what she was. But skin like that and eyes like blue stars are what the Others look like. And the tales call her the corpse queen. He brought her back through the Wall to the Nightfort, and proclaimed her a queen, and himself her king. With strange sorceries, he bound his sworn brothers to his will. The men who swore to guard the realms of men now served a king of the night. For thirteen years, Night's King and his corpse queen ruled the Wall.
CA: Before we find out who brought him down, and what they found when they did: if you want Westeros the way Martin wrote it, subscribe to the Mythic Archives.
III: His fall took something the North had never seen before: an alliance between enemies. The King of Winter in Winterfell, and Joramun, King-beyond-the-Wall, the wildling who, legends say, blew the Horn of Winter and woke giants from the earth. A Stark and a wildling. Men who had fought each other for generations, now marching together against the Watch itself. They broke the Night's King, and freed his brothers from their bondage. Then they discovered what he had been doing all those years. He had been making sacrifices to the Others. So every record of him was destroyed. His deeds were struck from the histories. Even his name was forbidden. That is why, eight thousand years later, nobody in Westeros knows what he was called.
IV: But Old Nan had an idea. She always ended the story the same way. "Some say he was a Bolton. Some say a Magnar out of Skagos, some say Umber, Flint, or Norrey. Some would have you think he was a Woodfoot, from them who ruled Bear Island." "He never was," she said. "He was a Stark, the brother of the man who brought him down." Then she pinched little Bran's nose. "He was a Stark of Winterfell, and who can say? Mayhaps his name was Brandon." She said one more thing, which Bran never forgot. "Night's King was only a man by light of day. But the night was his to rule." It is not a strange guess. House Stark has always loved the name. Brandon the Builder. Brandon the Shipwright, who sailed west and never returned. Brandon the Burner. Bran's own uncle Brandon. A Stark brother bringing down a Stark brother. The family whose words are "Winter is coming" may have given the Others their greatest ally.
V: The Nightfort still has one secret. In its kitchens there is an old well, and at the bottom of the well, there is a door. The Watch calls it the Black Gate. But it isn't black at all. It is pale white weirwood, glowing like milk and moonlight, and it has a face. When Bran's party reaches it, the face opens its eyes. "Who are you?" it asks. A brother of the Watch, Samwell Tarly, answers with the words of his oath. "I am the sword in the darkness. I am the watcher on the walls. I am the shield that guards the realms of men." "Then pass," the door says. Its mouth opens wide, and they walk through, under the Wall, into the North. A secret door through the Wall, in the castle where a Lord Commander once let the cold inside. The books never connect the two. But it is hard not to wonder.
VI: Then, in 2014, the show gave the name to someone new. In the fourth season, a White Walker rides through the snow carrying a baby to an altar of ice. A crown of icy horns rises from his head. He touches the child's cheek, and its eyes turn blue. HBO's official guide briefly named him the Night's King, then quietly removed the name. The show's version became its great villain. At Hardhome, he lifts his arms and the dead rise to join him. Beyond the Wall, he brings down one of Daenerys's dragons and raises it as his own. In the sixth season, the show reveals his origin. Long ago, the children of the forest bound a man of the First Men to a weirwood tree and drove a blade of dragonglass into his heart. He became the first White Walker. At Winterfell, in the final season, Arya Stark kills him with a Valyrian steel dagger, and his entire army falls with him. None of that happens in the books.
VII: When fans asked Martin whether the show's Night King and the book's Night's King were the same person, he gave a careful answer. "As for the Night's King, the form I prefer, in the books he is a legendary figure, akin to Lann the Clever and Brandon the Builder, and no more likely to have survived to the present day than they have." In other words, the Night's King of the books is a legend, like the trickster who stole Casterly Rock and the builder of the Wall. He may never even have existed. Notice the name, too. Martin prefers Night's King, with an S, like a title. The show dropped the S. And the books have no Night King at all. No one in the novels knows who leads the Others, or whether anyone does. No one knows where they came from. The children of the forest creating them is the show's idea, not Martin's.
VIII: But Martin's books are full of legends that turn out to be real. In the last published novel, a strange rider guides Bran north. He wears the black of the Night's Watch, rides a great elk, and hides his face behind a scarf. His hands are black, and cold as iron. He cannot cross the Wall. "There are spells woven into it," he says, "old ones, and strong." The children of the forest put it more simply: "They killed him long ago." Readers call him Coldhands. Some believe he is a forgotten brother of the Watch. A few wonder if he is something older. And beyond the Wall, the wildlings have been searching for something. "We opened half a hundred graves," the wildling girl Ygritte cries, "and never found the Horn of Joramun." The horn of the very king who brought down the Night's King. Martin has explained none of it. The Winds of Winter, the book that should bring the Long Night, is still unpublished, fifteen years after the last. So for now, the Night's King remains what Old Nan made him. A man by day. A legend by night. And a Stark, perhaps, whose name was Brandon.
